transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we are examining a shift in how coastal and riverside cities manage heavy storm runoff.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: For most of the twentieth century, engineers relied on concrete floodwalls and straight drainage channels to push rainwater away as fast as possible.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: However, when extreme rainfall overwhelms those rigid pipes, floodwater backs up into basements and subways.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Instead, many planners now design sunken parks—sometimes called sponge parks—with permeable soil, native reeds, and terraced paths.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: During dry weeks, families use the fields for picnics and running. When a storm arrives, the park intentionally floods, holding thousands of cubic meters of water until drains recover.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Every November, when rain streaked the brass sign above his shop, Arthur opened the cloth-bound ledger his grandfather had started in 1928.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Each page recorded not merely pocket watches and spring tensions, but brief notes about the owners: a ferry captain's salt-stained chronometer, a violinist's silver pendant watch.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That Tuesday, a young archivist stepped inside carrying a wrapped parcel and asked whether a tarnished railway watch could still keep honest time.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Arthur turned the dial toward the lamp, spotted the tiny serial number etched inside the case, and smiled—because that very number appeared on page twelve of the ledger.
